transcript.text: my mums got an old indesit dryer the white one with the dial, IDV75. it smells a bit hot when its on. someone at work said these catch fire?? is that true

⚠ Stop using this appliance
A burning or hot-plastic smell, smoke, scorching or melting can mean an electrical fault or a fire risk. Stop using it, switch it off and unplug it (or turn it off at the fuse box), and don't run it again — not even as a test — until it has been checked by a qualified engineer. Sadly, your colleague has a point. A few years ago Indesit, Hotpoint, Creda, Swan and Proline vented and condenser dryers made roughly 2004 to 2015 were part of a big safety modification programme, later made a formal recall. The issue was fluff touching the heating element and catching fire, and an older white Indesit with a dial, like an IDV75, is very much the type that was included. I can't say for certain that your mum's particular machine is affected, but a hot smell on one of these needs taking seriously. Please have her stop using it and keep it unplugged at the wall until a qualified engineer has checked it. Don't run another cycle to see if the smell comes back. The most likely causes of a hot smell, in order:
1. Fluff built up around the heater or in the air path, from a full filter or a squashed or blocked vent hose. This is the classic fire risk.
2. The dryer being one of the unmodified models from the safety programme, where that fluff problem is the known design fault.
3. Less likely, the thermostat or thermal cut-out not controlling the heat properly. Things you can safely do with it unplugged, to give the engineer a clear picture:
1. Find the serial number on the label inside the door rim. Enter it into the Whirlpool UK dryer safety checker (search "Whirlpool tumble dryer safety") or look it up on GOV.UK product safety alerts. If it says the dryer is affected and hasn't been modified, the manufacturer should arrange a fix or replacement free of charge. Modified machines usually have a small green dot or sticker near the label.
2. Pull out the fluff filter in the door opening. If it's heavily packed or the area behind it is furry with lint, that points strongly to overheating from blocked airflow.
3. Look at the vent hose at the back. It should be short, unkinked and not full of fluff. A crushed or clogged hose makes the heat build up. If it turns out to be an affected model, go through the manufacturer's programme. If not, a qualified engineer should still check the heater area and thermostats before it's used. On a dryer this old, if the repair isn't covered, replacing it is often the more sensible option. What does the checker say once you've put the serial number in?

mum cant read the little label and she cant pull it out to look at the back, so I dont have the serial, just IDV75 off the front. its in her kitchen and she does sometimes run it and go out, which worries me. she'll be annoyed but I'll tell her to unplug it now. what do we do without the serial?

⚠ Stop using this appliance
Unplugging it now is the right call, even if she's annoyed. A dryer that smells hot and is sometimes left running in an empty house is exactly the situation to avoid. 1. Read the label yourself when you're next there. On most dryers like this it's a sticker on the rim of the door opening, on the cabinet or the door edge, so you only need to open the door. You don't have to move the machine. If the print is tiny, take a close-up photo on your phone and zoom in. A small green dot or sticker near it usually means it's already been modified.
2. Or ring the manufacturer's dryer safety helpline. Search "Whirlpool tumble dryer recall" for the official number. Tell them it's an Indesit IDV75 vented dryer that smells hot. They can talk you through finding the serial and tell you whether it's covered. If it is and hasn't been fixed, they arrange a free modification or replacement offer.
3. If you book an engineer instead, they can read the serial and check it against the recall as part of the visit. A hot smell on one of these is most likely fluff building up around the heater or in the airflow. Less likely, a thermostat isn't controlling the heat properly. Both need proper checking, not another run. The vent hose at the back can wait for the engineer, since your mum can't get to it. The fluff filter in the door is easy to look at, though, and tells us a lot. If it's thickly packed, blocked airflow is the most likely cause of the heat. If it's fairly clean, that points more towards the hose, a build-up deeper inside, or the thermostat side. On a dryer this old, if it isn't covered by the recall, replacing it is usually more sensible than paying for repairs.
